paras: The lynching of John Mullins was the shooting of a Black man by a crowd of about fifteen men at his sister's house on Topisaw, near Tyler's mill, Mississippi, on the night of August 10, 1882. Mullins had been accused of attempting an outrage on a white woman in Lawrence County, and the local paper reported his killing under the heading "The Perpetrator Summarily Dealt with."

According to the Brookhaven Ledger, about a week and a half before the killing Mullins was accused of attempting "a nameless outrage" on Mrs. Smith, wife of Thos. Smith, who lived in southwestern Lawrence County near the Lincoln County line. Smith rode after him on horseback and shot him in the leg and again in the body, but Mullins escaped and hid in a sinkhole while Smith passed near him several times. Once things were quiet he dragged himself to a nearby Black household, and from there he was carried to his sister's house on Topisaw, which the Ledger placed "in this county."

On Thursday night, August 10, a crowd of men, "supposed to be about fifteen," came to the house and first called for his brother Mike Mullins, who was not there. When they called for John and were told he could not get up, they ordered him to sit up in bed, pulled two boards from the side of the house, and fired two shots into him through the opening. The men then ordered the people inside to cover their heads "under penalty of death," and three of them entered and fired twice more into Mullins, though the Ledger thought the shots from outside had already killed him. Before riding away, they crossed his hands and closed his eyes.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution of the men appears in the coverage, and none of them was named.

The Brookhaven Ledger broke the story on August 17 under the headlines "Atempt to Commit an Outrage" and "The Perpetrator Summarily Dealt with," presenting the accusation as fact. The Pascagoula Democrat-Star reprinted the Ledger text almost word for word and without credit on August 25. The Southern Herald of Liberty condensed the case on August 26 into two sentences among its "Editorial Items," calling Mullins "a negro" and the woman "a white lady." None of the three papers questioned the killing or the accusation, and the episode drew no Black-press coverage in the available sources, which begin in 1900.

The Herald said the crowd "captured Mullins and shot him to death" and placed the case in Lawrence County, while the more detailed Ledger account describes no capture, only a shooting in his sister's house in the Ledger's own county.

reader.title: Lynching of John Mullins
bases: A crowd of about fifteen men went at night to the house where John Mullins, a Black man accused of an attempted outrage, lay wounded and shot him to death (A4, A8).
Mullins was shot to death by a crowd of about fifteen men acting without any legal authority, in retaliation for an alleged attempted outrage on a white woman (A4, A8).

All the detail comes from the Brookhaven Ledger (A4); the Democrat-Star printed its text verbatim (A6) and the Southern Herald's two-sentence item (A8) agrees on the core facts but may be a condensation of the same report.
